title: Strat Chat - Checking for Understanding
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Opening a new 'Strat Chat' series, Shaun Brien tackles the why of checking for understanding (CfU) before getting into technique. He first clears away three common misconceptions: a CfU is not a check for learning (learning is a durable change in long-term memory that requires rehearsal over time, not a single in-class attempt), not a check for opinion (confidence surveys and thumbs-up/down polls measure what students think the teacher wants to hear, not actual understanding), and not a single closed question like 'does that make sense?' (which invites no honest negative answer and leaves most of the class unaccountable). Positively, he defines CfU as a whole-class task with no opportunity to opt out, framed as a diagnostic on the effectiveness of the teacher's instruction rather than a verdict on students. Brien then introduces the TAPPLE technique (Teach, Ask a question, Pause/Pair-share, Pick a non-volunteer, Listen, Effective feedback/Elaborate) as the practical mechanism for implementing this in a lesson, with particular emphasis on cold-calling non-volunteers to keep the whole class accountable and on echoing/elaborating on responses so the full class hears and can probe the reasoning behind an answer.
points: Sharp distinction between learning and performance: a single correct in-class response after instruction does not indicate the knowledge has transferred to long-term memory, which requires rehearsal and retrieval over time.

Rejects confidence-based checks (thumbs up/down, traffic lights, 'does that make sense?') as unreliable because students tend to signal what they think the teacher wants to see rather than reveal genuine understanding.

Reframes checking for understanding as a diagnostic on the teacher's instruction, not a test of the student -- its purpose is to determine whether intervention is needed before moving on, not to grade comprehension.

Introduces TAPPLE (Teach, Ask, Pause/Pair-share, Pick a non-volunteer, Listen, Effective feedback) as a structured, no-opt-out routine that keeps every student accountable rather than relying on eager volunteers.

Cites the principle that cold-calling non-volunteers, rather than taking hands-up answers, is essential because volunteer-only questioning signals to the rest of the class that they don't need to think.
quotes: [1] "A check for understanding is a powerful teaching tool not for checking for student learning, for checking the effectiveness of the instruction throughout the lesson and determining whether intervention is required before moving on.

[2] "A check for understanding is not a check for learning. It is important to distinguish between learning and performance. Learning is a change in long term memory and it's highly unlikely that by attempting a problem once in class... that the transfer to long term memory will occur.

[3] "Students completing a confidence survey where they tell you whether they understand or not using a mechanism like traffic lights, thumbs up/down, fist to five is not actually showing you understanding. It's likely to actually be showing you what the students think you want to see or hear so that you'll move on.
[4] "If you're not checking for understanding you're just guessing, and guessing isn't teaching. - Anna Stokke

[5] "Sure those eager hands are often a delight in the classroom and they're usually going to give you the correct answer, but what about everybody else? If you're picking from volunteers then you're sending a message to the rest of the class that they do not need to think and respond because you're not going to ask them.

[6] "'I don't know' is actually an acceptable answer from a student here, but it is not a get out of jail free card. If they do not know simply tell them that it is okay that they do not know but you are going to ask a few other students and then come back to them.
